questions.q: Why does this lesson avoid stating one fixed number for an org's daily API request allocation?
options: Because API limits don't actually exist in Salesforce
Because the allocation depends on the org's edition and the number/type of licenses it holds, so there is no single number true for every org
Because the allocation changes randomly every day with no pattern
Because only sandboxes have API limits, not production orgs
questions.explain: The actual allocation varies by edition and licensing, so the reliable way to know it is to check the org's own /limits resource rather than memorize a figure.

options: Only the org's remaining API requests, with no other information
A list of every user currently logged in
A family of named limits (API requests, data storage, concurrent report instances, and more), each with a Max and Remaining value
The org's SOQL query history
questions.explain: /limits covers many named limits beyond just API requests, each reported as a Max/Remaining pair.

questions.q: What happens when an org exhausts its daily API request allocation?
options: Calls succeed but run slower
The org is permanently locked out of the API
Only write operations fail; reads continue working normally
Further calls fail with 403 Forbidden and errorCode REQUEST_LIMIT_EXCEEDED until the rolling window frees some allocation back up
questions.explain: There's no partial degradation — once the allocation is spent, further calls fail with that specific error until the 24-hour rolling window recovers capacity.

questions.q: Which practice does this lesson recommend to reduce API consumption for detecting changes, instead of repeatedly querying to check?
options: Using Platform Events or Change Data Capture to get pushed a notification only when something actually changes
Polling /query every second instead of every minute
Disabling the /limits resource
Switching from REST to SOAP, which has no request limits
questions.explain: Event-driven approaches eliminate the wasted calls that polling makes even when nothing has changed, which is the core inefficiency polling creates.

questions.q: Why is using Bulk API 2.0 for a large data load a better practice than looping single-record REST calls, from an API-limit perspective?
options: Bulk API 2.0 jobs don't count against the org's API allocation at all
Bulk API 2.0 is only available to orgs with unlimited API requests
REST calls cannot create records at all
A single bulk job consumes far fewer requests than making one REST call per record across a large dataset
questions.explain: Submitting one asynchronous job instead of thousands of individual REST calls dramatically reduces the number of requests consumed for the same volume of data.
